clue.text: Handy snack?

parts.note: 'handy' reads as 'eaten with the hands': a party nibble held in the fingers rather than with cutlery

explanation.definitionFit: Canapés and sandwiches eaten by hand at a party are called by this name.

clue.text: Clown is briefly involved in fund-raising event

indicators.note: being involved in something here means being placed inside the event's word

parts.note: a fete is an outdoor fund-raising fair
'is' shortened to its contraction, as in it's, leaves just S

explanation.surface: A clown turns up as part of the entertainment at a charity fair.
explanation.walkthrough: A fete is a British outdoor fair held to raise money. 'Involved in' puts S inside FETE.
explanation.definitionFit: Feste is the jester, the professional fool, in Shakespeare's Twelfth Night.

clue.text: It's awkward, being out

definitions.meaning: ill at ease, uncomfortable in a situation
away from the house, not in

explanation.definitionFit: The phrase means both ill at ease, as in feeling unfamiliar, and literally absent from the house when someone calls.

clue.text: At a loss for words?

parts.note: 'words' stand for expressions, so being without them describes a blank, deadpan face

explanation.definitionFit: A face showing no feeling is blank or deadpan, literally lacking expressions, which the clue calls words.

clue.text: Swimmer absorbs local European language

indicators.note: the swimmer takes the pub into itself, so one word goes inside the other

parts.note: a fish is a swimmer
a local is a British pub, here an inn

explanation.surface: A swimmer picks up some of the regional European tongue.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Local' is British slang for one's nearby pub, an INN; 'absorbs' puts it inside FISH after the F.
explanation.definitionFit: The tongue of Finland is a Finno-Ugric language of northern Europe.

clue.text: Solo dance?

parts.note: 'solo' suggests one person, but read as one pace it names a quick ballroom dance of the 1910s

explanation.definitionFit: This ragtime-era ballroom dance takes one pace per beat, so a single step is the dance itself.

clue.text: Drop round for dessert

parts.note: to sag is to droop or drop
O is round in shape

explanation.surface: Popping round to someone's house in time for pudding.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Drop round' reads as a visit, but it splits into SAG and O.
explanation.definitionFit: This starchy palm pith is cooked with milk into a pudding served after the main course.

clue.text: Honour note after trouble

indicators.note: the note follows the trouble, so its letters come second

parts.note: ado is fuss or trouble
re is the second note of the sol-fa scale

explanation.surface: A tribute paid by letter once the trouble has passed.
explanation.definitionFit: To revere or worship someone is to give them great honour.

clue.text: Charge is a mistake

definitions.meaning: supervision, responsibility for looking after something
an error caused by failing to notice something

explanation.definitionFit: The word means both supervision of something in one's care and a slip made by not noticing.

clue.text: I resent Alfred's striving to be in control

indicators.note: the letters struggle and twist about, so they are rearranged

explanation.surface: Someone resents Alfred's ambitious efforts to take charge.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Striving' shuffles all the letters of I RESENT ALFREDS, including the S of the possessive.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone who holds back their impulses keeps themselves in check.

clue.text: Determined to make arrangement acceptable

parts.note: a setup is an arrangement or organisation
'on' means acceptable, as in 'that's not on'

explanation.surface: Resolved to get some plan agreed.
explanation.definitionFit: Being bent on doing something means being resolved to do it.

clue.text: Ugly feature, certainly nothing put in before

indicators.note: these words are set inside another word

parts.note: ere is an old word for before
yes means certainly
O looks like zero, nothing

explanation.surface: A blemish on the landscape, put in place long ago.
explanation.definitionFit: A building or sight that spoils its surroundings is something unpleasant to look at.

clue.text: Radical to the last?

parts.note: someone holding views at the far end, the last point, of the spectrum, perhaps one who stays radical until death

explanation.definitionFit: A person with radical views goes to the extreme, the furthest point.

clue.text: Is anxious about dividing newspaper society

indicators.note: one piece splits another by sitting in its middle

parts.note: FT is the Financial Times
re means about, concerning

explanation.surface: Someone worries over a report that splits the press and high society.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Dividing' puts RE between the F and T of FT, then S follows.
explanation.definitionFit: To fret is to worry.

clue.text: Indicates disapproval about the northern hotel worker

indicators.note: the disapproval wraps around the northern word

parts.note: boos signal disapproval
in Yorkshire and other northern English dialects 'the' is shortened to t'

explanation.surface: Someone jeers at the hotel porter from the north.
explanation.walkthrough: Boots was the old British name for the hotel servant who cleaned guests' shoes.
explanation.definitionFit: The servant who polished guests' footwear in a hotel was named for that job.

clue.text: Flower that's flatter round top of calyx

indicators.note: the flattery goes round the letter taken from calyx

parts.note: to butter up is to flatter

indicators.note: the top of a down clue word is its first letter

explanation.surface: A bloom whose sepals look as if they have been flattened at the top.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Round' puts C inside BUTTER UP, between its two words.
explanation.definitionFit: This yellow meadow plant of the genus Ranunculus is a familiar wild bloom.

clue.text: Fashionable event taking place

explanation.definitionFit: The word means trendy, an occurrence or improvised show, and occurring, three senses side by side.

clue.text: Working together and playing together?

definitions.meaning: performing live music at a show

explanation.definitionFit: The phrase means acting in cooperation and, literally, performing at a live musical show.

clue.text: Windsors set off rashly to east

indicators.note: the letters are set off, set going in a new order

parts.note: E is the compass abbreviation for east

explanation.surface: Members of a family setting out hastily for the east.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Set off' looks like the travelling verb but rearranges RASHLY, TO and E.
explanation.definitionFit: Windsor is the surname of the British monarch's family.

clue.text: Warn about incorporating British province in Canada

indicators.note: the warning takes in the British abbreviation

parts.note: to alert is to warn
a is an abbreviation for about, used in dates

explanation.surface: A warning about a British province in Canada.
explanation.definitionFit: This western prairie region, capital Edmonton, is one of the Canadian provinces.

clue.text: Grains of doubt?

definitions.meaning: an apothecaries' weight equal to twenty grains, so the plural matches the unit's size

explanation.definitionFit: It is both an old apothecaries' measure of twenty grains and a qualm that stops someone acting.

clue.text: Understood one's in time to take effect

indicators.note: the one is placed inside the other letters

parts.note: to act is to take effect, as a medicine does
I is the Roman numeral one

explanation.surface: One arrives just in time for something to start working.
explanation.definitionFit: Tacit agreement is implied without being spoken.

clue.text: Run into one coming back for list

indicators.note: returning means the built word is read backwards
the run goes inside the other word

parts.note: lone means one, single
R is the cricket abbreviation for run

explanation.surface: A runner collides with someone returning to sign up.
explanation.walkthrough: R inside LONE gives LORNE, which 'coming back' turns round.
explanation.definitionFit: To enrol is to put a name on a register, to list it.

clue.text: Move round under cover of manoeuvre

indicators.note: the round letter hides inside the trick, beneath its cover

parts.note: a ruse is a trick or manoeuvre
O is round in shape

explanation.surface: Troops move around under cover of a military manoeuvre.
explanation.definitionFit: To rouse is to stir someone, to move them to action.

clue.text: Drawing-pin?

parts.note: not a thumbtack but a pin-shaped rod that draws iron towards it

explanation.definitionFit: A straight rod-shaped magnet draws metal objects to it, a pin that does the drawing.

clue.text: Sum child's given by a student

parts.note: a tot is a small child
L is a learner driver's plate, so a student

explanation.surface: A youngster's arithmetic is handed to a pupil.
explanation.definitionFit: A total is the whole amount when figures are added up.

clue.text: I'll leave guide holding small horse

indicators.note: the remaining letters hold the small abbreviation inside
the I departs from the guide's word

parts.note: a courier is a tour guide

explanation.surface: A tour guide quits, left with only a little pony.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Leave' takes I out of COURIER to give COURER; 'holding' puts S inside it.
explanation.definitionFit: A courser is a poetic word for a swift horse, especially a warhorse.

clue.text: Keen on getting new data into place

indicators.note: these letters go inside the word for place

parts.note: to put is to place
gen is British slang for information

explanation.surface: Eager to get fresh figures entered in their slot.
explanation.walkthrough: GEN is British slang for information, as in 'get the gen'.
explanation.definitionFit: A keen smell or wit is sharp, biting.

clue.text: Going around castle, take a look

indicators.note: turning around means the word is read backwards

parts.note: the keep is the main tower of a castle

explanation.surface: Walking round the fortress, have a glance.
explanation.definitionFit: A peek is a quick glance.

clue.text: Priestly red coat's torn by a novice

indicators.note: the coat is ripped apart, so its letters are rearranged

parts.note: L is a learner, a novice

explanation.surface: A priest's red vestment is ripped by a beginner.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Torn' rearranges REDCOATS and A; the S of the possessive counts.
explanation.definitionFit: Sacerdotal describes things belonging to the priesthood.
